User Information-Seeking Behaviour in the Generative AI Era


Within the context of academic libraries, several studies have explored users’ information-seeking
behaviour, with growing attention to information literacy practices in the era of generative AI (Frenkel et
al., 2024; Patel & Kamboya, 2025; Sebastian, 2025). Frenkel et al. (2024), studying engineering students
and faculty, found that respondents who used ChatGPT for academic or research purposes generally
perceived it as accurate, helpful, and capable of addressing a wide range of engineering-related topics.
Their findings suggest that the adoption of generative AI is likely to increase in academic environments.


Patel and Kamboya (2025) similarly report that generative AI can streamline the information-seeking
process by making searches faster and more efficient than traditional methods. They note that these
developments present important considerations for libraries as they adapt their services and instructional
approaches in response to emerging AI tools. Sebastian (2025) challenges traditional information-seeking
behaviour models and argues that they are insufficient in the age of generative AI. Informed by queer

                                                                                           33                                                             Evidence Based Library and Information Practice 2026, 21.3



theory, the author advocates for a shift toward a more humanistic approach by embracing uncertainty,
performativity, and embodied subjectivity.


Research Guides From Pathfinders to Online Learning Tools


Evolving patterns of information-seeking behaviour have implications for library tools designed to
support research and learning, including research guides. Research guides have played a central role in
academic libraries by helping students navigate curated sets of resources on specific topics within the
broader context of information literacy (Smith, 2008). Historically rooted in print bibliographies and
pathfinders, early guides consisted of structured list of books and reference materials and later expanded
to include subject headings, journals, proceedings, and other discipline-specific resources (Jackson &
Pellack, 2004; Smith, 2008). With the rise of search engines and the shift toward web-based discovery,
these tools moved online (Smith, 2008; Vileno, 2007). A growing body of research has examined best
practices related to the user experience and pedagogical value of research guides (Barker & Hoffman,
2021; Crego-Emley & Lambaria, 2024; Crenshaw & Johnson, 2024; Lee & Lowe, 2018; Logan & Spence,
2021), as well as challenges inherent in their deployment, including workload, perceived usefulness,
accessibility, and limited student awareness (Bergstrom-Lynch, 2019; Carey et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2019;
Chee & Weaver, 2021; Conerton & Goldenstein, 2017; Vileno, 2007).


A review of the literature on the history of research guides revealed a consistent set of concerns regarding
their visibility, audience, and effectiveness. As early as 2007, Vileno questioned whether librarians were
creating online research guides primarily for other librarians rather than for library users, who may not
be aware of these resources, and raised several questions on their content, design, marketing, and use in
instruction. Nearly two decades later, these questions remain highly relevant. Today, however, they are
further complicated by a rapidly evolving technological landscape being shaped by generative AI.


To our knowledge, no empirical study has yet examined the relationship between generative AI and the
use of research guides. This exploratory study addresses this gap by evaluating whether research guide
usage reflects broader declines in web traffic, whether usage patterns shifted following the introduction
of ChatGPT, and whether there were changes in how users accessed the guides.


Methods


Web traffic data were selected as the primary source of evidence for this study because they provide an
objective measure of user engagement with the library’s online research guides (Fagan, 2014; Turner,
2010). These data capture actual patterns of access and interaction, such as frequency and referral sources,
which allows for a quantitative assessment of user behaviour over time. This approach enables the
identification of usage trends and potential shifts associated with the introduction of generative AI tools.


The dataset for published guides at the University of Ottawa Library, comprising monthly aggregate
view counts from the LibGuides platform, was initially obtained on June 4, 2025, and covered the period
from June 2015 through May 2025. Traffic source data were retrieved from Google Analytics, which
provides detailed referral information not available within the LibGuides platform. The Google Analytics
datasets were downloaded on August 13, 2025, and covered the period from May 2023 to May 2025 (no
data were available prior to May 2023).


Data analysis was conducted using RStudio Desktop, an integrated development environment for R, a
programming language designed for statistical computing and graphics.

To extend the analysis through the end of 2025, updated datasets were downloaded from LibGuides on

December 2025. The same analytical code was applied to the updated dataset, which forms the basis of
the findings reported in this study. To support transparency and reproducibility, the full dataset and all
analysis scripts have been archived in Borealis (Lee, 2026).


A total 297 published guides were downloaded from the LibGuides platform. Five of these were redirects
to other guides (IDs: 739278, 742981, 588665, 724195, and 588675) and were excluded from the analysis.
This resulted in a final analytical sample of 292 guides.


Data from 2015 were excluded from analysis of overall traffic trends, since this year only had partial data.
Of note, the dataset included all published guides, some of which were created partway through the
study period. To more accurately capture the number of active guides per year, the first month in which
each guide recorded traffic was used as a proxy for its creation date.


The datasets were assessed to examine overall trends in web traffic to the research guides before and after
the introduction of ChatGPT. Since ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022, two equivalent periods
were selected for comparison: November 2019 to November 2022 (37 months) representing the pre-

session medium, sessions, and engaged sessions. Session source identifies the origin of traffic (e.g.,

because they offer direct insight into how users accessed the research guides and the extent to which they

{"answer": "# Generative AI and the economics of open infrastructure

**Bottom line.** Generative AI raises the usefulness of open code, data and scientific literature, but it can separate *use of an open resource* from *visits, contributions, revenue and feedback received by its producer*. At the same time, automated collection and submission can increase hosting and review costs. These are shifts in bargaining power and unit economics, not evidence that openness has stopped creating value—or that every AI-assisted contribution is harmful. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000012)

The principal mechanisms and their evidentiary limits are summarized below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## Where the value goes

**Open code becomes a model input.** BigCode assembled *The Stack* from approximately 3.1 TB of permissively licensed source code and used it to train the publicly released StarCoder family; StarCoderBase was trained on one trillion tokens from GitHub repositories. The project provided inspection, opt-out and attribution tools, illustrating a reciprocal model. Commercial coding assistants also draw on public-code ecosystems, but these studies do **not** establish how much of any assistant’s revenue is attributable to particular repositories or how much reaches their maintainers. A platform controlling the assistant, customer relationship and distribution can monetize capabilities derived partly from code maintained elsewhere. Public availability of code is not, by itself, evidence that every training or output use complies with its license. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000020)

**Open science supplies inputs—and can receive valuable outputs.** Decades of publicly deposited protein structures and sequence research underpinned DeepMind’s AlphaFold. Google DeepMind and EMBL–EBI subsequently made more than 214 million predicted structures accessible through the AlphaFold database, which DeepMind funds: this is a substantial return to the research commons, not an example of a demonstrated AlphaFold subscription business. In biomedicine, the BIOMEDICA researchers converted over six million articles in PubMed Central’s open-access subset into more than 24 million image–caption pairs, then released a dataset, code and trained models. These examples show that the organization building an AI layer may gain model expertise, distribution or downstream application opportunities, while scientists and the public can also gain genuinely open assets; neither example quantifies a transfer of profit away from the original data stewards. (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000022)

That distinction matters economically: the costs of producing, validating, updating and serving source data remain with laboratories, repositories, publishers and contributors even when a downstream model makes the information easier to consume elsewhere. An analysis of reported AI training-data transactions found several pricing arrangements but that most documented deals excluded original creators from compensation; its deal sample should not be interpreted as a measured revenue share for *all* open-science or open-source producers. (pqac-00000056)

## Demand, participation and operating costs

**AI answers can displace the visit and the public question.** A difference-in-differences study estimated that Stack Overflow’s weekly questions-and-answers fell about **16%** relative to comparison forums after ChatGPT launched, reaching roughly **25% within six months**. Votes on remaining posts did not materially improve, so the evidence does not support assuming that only trivial or low-quality contributions disappeared. A separate study found declines in Stack Overflow visits and questions but no comparable participation decline in the Reddit developer communities examined; it also found greater exit among newer Stack Overflow users. The loss at issue is not just a page view: a privately resolved question no longer automatically becomes a searchable answer, contributor interaction or fresh training example for the public commons. These are comparative observational studies, not proof that ChatGPT explains every subsequent decline. (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004)

Evidence for **documentation traffic specifically is narrower**. In a single-institution study of University of Ottawa library research guides—a form of open research documentation—**175 of 210** guides had fewer views across matched pre- and post-ChatGPT periods, with a **median change of −38.35%**. This is a before/after association, not a causal estimate for ChatGPT or a measured decline for software documentation generally. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000012)

| Mechanism | Key measured observation | Investor interpretation and qualification |
|---|---|---|

The same open-code ecosystem supports commercial tools such as Copilot, but the evidence does not quantify how value is divided between vendors and contributors. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024) | Openness enables public innovation and private capture. Favor businesses with defensible workflow, distribution, support, or proprietary context—not merely access to open code. |
| Open-science data and reciprocal value | PDB’s open structures were indispensable to structure-prediction tools; Google DeepMind funds the open AlphaFold database, which contains over 214 million predictions. BIOMEDICA converted more than 6 million PMC articles into 24 million image-text pairs and released data, code, and models. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059) | Value is not solely captured privately: AI projects can return major research assets to the commons. Assess whether commercial beneficiaries fund stewardship and produce useful open outputs. |

In an observational Ottawa study, 175 of 210 research guides lost traffic; the median change was −38.35% across matched pre/post periods. Additional post-release changes included a systematic increase in the average tenure of Stack Overflow accounts posting questions, consistent with newer and less expert users reducing participation or exiting, and an increase in question complexity as measured by the prevalence of words with six or more characters. contexts.context: Del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva, and Wachs provide quantitative primary evidence that ChatGPT reduced activity on Stack Overflow relative to comparison platforms. Using a difference-in-differences design, they compare weekly Stack Overflow posting activity with four comparable Q&A sites selected because ChatGPT access was limited for some users or because it performed less well on the relevant topics. They estimate an approximately 16% decline in weekly posts after ChatGPT’s release, growing to about 25% within six months. The effect is larger for widely used programming languages, including Python and JavaScript. Stable voting scores for posts published before and after the release suggest that the decline was not limited to duplicate or low-quality questions and answers, although votes are only a simple measure of content quality. Methodological caveats include reliance on observational comparison groups and the assumption that these platforms provide valid counterfactual trends; the excerpt does not establish that ChatGPT caused every observed change. The study concerns Stack Overflow posts, not visits specifically, and provides no evidence here about documentation traffic, Wikipedia traffic, AI Overviews, GitHub Copilot contributions, AI-generated pull requests or bug reports, or crawler-induced bandwidth costs on Wikimedia, arXiv, or scholarly infrastructure.

contexts.context: Burtch, Lee, and Chen provide quantitative primary evidence on Stack Overflow following ChatGPT’s late-November 2022 release. Using proprietary daily aggregate visitor counts from September 2022 through March 2023 and Stack Exchange Data Explorer data on questions, answers, and user characteristics for comparable October–mid-March periods in 2021–2022 and 2022–2023, they report significant declines in Stack Overflow visits and question volumes. The reduction was especially pronounced in topics where ChatGPT was likely more capable, and newer, less socially embedded users were most likely to leave. The authors also report that questions remaining after release became more complex and sophisticated. Reddit developer communities serve as a contrasting context: the excerpt reports no detectable participation decline there, which the authors attribute to stronger social bonds and a greater role for social fabric than on Stack Overflow’s primarily informational platform. Methodological caveats visible in this excerpt include the observational before/after design around ChatGPT’s release, reliance on proprietary traffic data, comparison of different calendar periods, and use of historical community data availability as a proxy for LLM capability/training-data exposure. The excerpt contains no evidence on documentation traffic, AI Overviews, GitHub Copilot, low-quality pull requests or bug reports, or AI crawler bandwidth costs for Wikimedia, arXiv, or other scholarly infrastructure.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general economic analysis relevant to commercial value capture, licensing, provenance, and attribution, but it does not directly document the requested individual texts, specific training-data sources, commercial-versus-public benefits, exact documentation traffic changes, or Wikimedia crawler bandwidth figures. It argues that training-data value is context-dependent: value depends on a buyer’s existing holdings and on how datasets combine during training, rather than on a dataset in isolation. It also identifies a transparency problem: buyers need to inspect data to assess its value, but inspection can enable copying. contexts.context: A June 2025 GLAM-E Lab survey found AI scraping bots threaten open cultural collections: 39/43 respondents saw recent traffic increases; 27 attributed them to AI-training bots and seven suspected them. Institutions often noticed only after servers were overwhelmed or collections went offline. Bots have operated since 2021, arrive in short, increasingly frequent swarms, often disguise their origins, ignore robots.txt, and can resemble distributed denial-of-service attacks. The report emphasizes infrastructure, analytics, and mitigation costs, while noting bots generally disregard licenses.

contexts.context: A study of 120,918 reports across 101 open-source projects (Jan 2024–Sep 2026) finds AI reports becoming more complete and valid, but still costly to verify. AI-assisted reproduction/diagnosis correlate with validity; AI-written reports do not. Maintainers spend more effort on AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than AI-discovered ones. Curl’s confirmed vulnerabilities fell below 5% amid low-quality submissions, then recovered to ~16% by April 2026; its maintainer later described “high volume, high quality.” The authors’ 53 AI-discovered reports achieved 69.81% acceptance.

contexts.context: StarCoder illustrates value capture from open code: BigCode trained a 15.5B-parameter model on **1 trillion tokens** from permissively licensed GitHub repositories in The Stack, then fine-tuned it on **35B Python tokens**. Microsoft Copilot has surpassed **1 million professional developers**, and users reportedly generate **35% of their code** with it, while lawsuits question whether developers’ public code can be commercially used for training. StarCoder’s creators added opt-out, PII redaction, attribution tracing, and a commercially viable open license, highlighting both benefits and legal risks of AI built on open-source contributions.

contexts.context: Lee and Smith’s University of Ottawa study analyzed 210 research guides across equivalent 37-month pre-/post-ChatGPT periods. Usage rose through 2022 but declined in 2023–25: 175 guides lost traffic, with a median change of −38.35% (range −91.3% to +462.7%). Google remained dominant, yet Google referrals fell while generative-AI referrals grew. The article links this to “zero-click searches,” where AI summaries answer queries without external visits. Related evidence reports an 8% year-over-year decline in human Wikipedia visits in 2025 and Pew found users less likely to click cited links when Google displayed AI summaries.

contexts.context: The study reports that GenAI lowers FOSS contribution barriers but increases maintainer workload. AI-slop PRs rose in mid-2025, peaking in May 2026; they were mostly additive, rarely merged, and usually closed within three days. Authors disclosed AI use in only 14% (another 1% after maintainer requests). Reasons included build failures and “looks AI to me.” Related evidence across 294 repositories found increased PR volume in 2025, declining merge rates, and especially lower success among one-time contributors. Researchers characterize this as a “tragedy of the commons” or DDoS-like pressure, contributing to review delays, maintenance labor, stress, and burnout.

contexts.context: METR’s 2025 randomized trial tested 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 real tasks (average two hours) in repositories averaging 23,000 stars. Contrary to expectations—developers predicted 24% faster completion, experts 38–39% faster—allowing Cursor Pro and Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet made tasks 19% slower; developers retrospectively estimated a 20% speedup. Participants had substantial prior LLM experience. Screen analysis covered 143 hours and found the slowdown robust across many checks, though setting-specific and not proof AI cannot help elsewhere. The evidence cautions investors against assuming coding assistants automatically reduce maintenance costs or increase open-source productivity.

The authors warn that foreclosure could bias AI diversity, freshness, and scaling, affecting commercial, nonprofit, and academic AI.

contexts.context: A 2026 study of Google AI Overviews (AIOs), reaching over 2 billion users, shows generative AI shifting value from publishers to platform intermediaries. Across 55,393 queries, AIOs appeared 13.7% overall and 64.7% for questions. They synthesized 98,020 claims; 11.0% were unsupported by cited pages. Although cited domains were more credible, 29.8% were absent from first-page results, indicating Google’s separate source-selection system. “Well over half” of cited pages carried advertising, yet summaries suppress click-through while Google’s sponsored ads remain, threatening publisher revenue and increasing Google’s editorial and economic control.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that publicly accessible open-source documentation is commonly crawled and incorporated into AI training, while updates may take months to reach models; retrieval tools such as Context7 address staleness. Stack Overflow data cited says 51% of professional developers use AI daily. AI agents compress multi-page documentation use into one or two requests, making conventional engagement metrics unreliable. Cloudflare found Bytespider, Amazonbot, and ClaudeBot/GPTBot among highest-volume crawlers; GPTBot requests grew over 300%, alongside an 18% annual rise in non-human traffic. SAP evidence suggests moderate GenAI improves efficiency, but excessive use reduces benefits.

The studies summarized here use different methodologies and populations, which limits direct causal comparison: Peng et al. use a controlled standardized HTTP-server task and report a 55.8% speed gain; Cui et al. use randomized field experiments involving 4,867 developers across three organizations and report 26.1% more completed tasks, while noting that only some work is amenable to AI assistance; Bakal et al. provide deployment statistics from more than 400 developers but do not constitute a randomized causal estimate; and Becker et al.’s METR randomized controlled trial finds experienced open-source developers were 19% slower. contexts.context: Raskin et al. provide a maintainer-identified, repository- and keyword-based estimate rather than a census or direct detector of all AI-generated contributions. The denominator is 10,000 repositories screened, of which 76 were identified as affected; most affected repositories had fewer than five slop PRs. The phenomenon first appears in July 2024 and does not increase significantly until mid-2025. These PRs are overwhelmingly rejected: fewer than 1% were merged, versus 84.73% of the non-slop baseline, while 97.8% were closed and typically processed within three to four days. The dataset contains important selection and measurement limitations. Seven PRs disappeared between mining and annotation, and potentially more may have been deleted before collection, producing survivorship bias. Mining depended on exploratory keywords and labels chosen by developers, so unrecognized cases are excluded. Reasons for flagging were often subjective, including whether work was pointless or merely “look AI,” and only 13.9% of PRs disclosed AI use (with another 1.6% disclosing it only after a maintainer request). The reported mid-2025 increase is correlational: the study cannot establish that adoption of agentic coding tools caused it. Thus, the findings quantify maintainer-perceived slop and rejection outcomes, not the prevalence or causal effects of AI coding generally.

contexts.context: The paper says foundation models ingested much of the public internet but use “less than 0.01%” of available data, leaving roughly 99% dark or proprietary. AI labs increasingly pursue private sources through deals worth “tens to hundreds of millions of dollars,” while “most deals exclude original creators from compensation.” Data is nonrival in principle and copies are easily made, but contamination (aging, poisoning, benchmark/preference leakage) creates practical rivalry. Inspection can enable “perfect replication,” and legal opacity, context dependence, and fragmented pricing make ownership and value capture difficult—relevant to open-code, open-data, and open-science producers.

contexts.context: A study of 229 OSS participants and 294 repositories describes AI-generated contributions as “AI-DDoS”: credible-looking submissions are cheap to produce, increasing review and maintenance burdens. Communities favor low-cost defenses—stricter CI gates (73%), no-review cutoffs (71%), AI-use disclosure (63%), pre-review gates (62%), and risk flags (58%)—but resist labor-intensive AI reviewers (48%) and expanded triage (34%). Some consider verifying contributor understanding (67%) or identity (39%). Respondents warn that such defenses may undermine “openness.” Findings are ecosystem-level, mainly from popular repositories, and issue-metric changes are interpreted cautiously.

contexts.context: A study mined 10,000 GitHub repositories for maintainer-identified AI “slop” pull requests (PRs), using titles/labels such as “slop,” “ai-spam,” and “ai junk.” It found 1,959 candidates; manual review removed 173 false positives (91.17% precision), leaving 1,786. Monthly slop PRs rose from 0–5 through September 2025 to 13, then 50 in October 2025. The study annotated AI disclosure, related issues, protests, flaggers/closers, bots, and maintainer reasons, evidencing increasing review and filtering work imposed on open-source maintainers.

contexts.context: Protein-structure AI illustrates how open science data can enable valuable downstream tools: decades of open sequence/structure research and resources such as PDB and UniProt supported AlphaFold, RoseTTAFold and OpenFold. AlphaFold’s database, a collaboration between EMBL-EBI and Google DeepMind, expanded from about 300,000 to over 214 million structures. Precomputed models save users hours of computation and reduce redundant large-scale calculations and carbon emissions, while enabling integration into UniProt, InterPro and Ensembl. Thus, organizations maintaining open data bear infrastructure costs, while AI developers and downstream users may capture substantial value.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: How is generative AI changing the economics and risks of open-source software, open data and open science for the organizations that produce them? Include evidence on AI models trained on open code and open scientific data (who captures the value), declines in community Q&A and documentation traffic after ChatGPT (for example studies of Stack Overflow), effects of AI coding assistants on open-source contribution and maintenance, load from AI crawlers on open infrastructure, AI-generated low-quality contributions and bug reports burdening maintainers, and whether AI lowers the cost of copying or re-implementing open products. What do these imply for investors in open-source or open-science businesses?

# Generative AI and the economics of open infrastructure

**Bottom line.** Generative AI raises the usefulness of open code, data and scientific literature, but it can separate *use of an open resource* from *visits, contributions, revenue and feedback received by its producer*. At the same time, automated collection and submission can increase hosting and review costs. These are shifts in bargaining power and unit economics, not evidence that openness has stopped creating value—or that every AI-assisted contribution is harmful. (li2023starcodermaythe pages 1-2, lozano2025biomedicaanopen pages 1-2, riochanona2024largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, noroozian2025generativeaiand pages 1-3, song2026theimpactof pages 1-4)

The principal mechanisms and their evidentiary limits are summarized below.

| Mechanism | Key measured observation | Investor interpretation and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Open-code training and value capture | StarCoderBase was trained on 1 trillion tokens from permissively licensed GitHub repositories; its model and attribution tools were released publicly. The same open-code ecosystem supports commercial tools such as Copilot, but the evidence does not quantify how value is divided between vendors and contributors. (li2023starcodermaythe pages 1-2, kocetkov2022thestack3 pages 1-3) | Openness enables public innovation and private capture. Favor businesses with defensible workflow, distribution, support, or proprietary context—not merely access to open code. |
| Open-science data and reciprocal value | PDB’s open structures were indispensable to structure-prediction tools; Google DeepMind funds the open AlphaFold database, which contains over 214 million predictions. BIOMEDICA converted more than 6 million PMC articles into 24 million image-text pairs and released data, code, and models. (lozano2025biomedicaanopen pages 1-2, varadi2024alphafoldproteinstructure pages 6-7, varadi2024alphafoldproteinstructure pages 1-2) | Value is not solely captured privately: AI projects can return major research assets to the commons. Assess whether commercial beneficiaries fund stewardship and produce useful open outputs. |
| Lost Q&A and documentation traffic | Stack Overflow posts fell an estimated 16% relative to controls after ChatGPT, reaching about 25% within six months. In an observational Ottawa study, 175 of 210 research guides lost traffic; the median change was −38.35% across matched pre/post periods. (riochanona2024largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, lee2026changingpatternsof pages 1-3, lee2026changingpatternsof pages 3-5) | AI can disintermediate audience, attribution, feedback, and contributor recruitment. The Stack Overflow result is quasi-experimental; the guide study does not prove that AI caused the decline. |
| Coding-assistant productivity and maintenance | Copilot use was associated with 5.9% more project-level OSS contributions but 8% more coordination time. In a separate randomized trial, 16 experienced developers completing 246 tasks in familiar projects were 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools. (song2026theimpactof pages 1-4, becker2507measuringtheimpact pages 1-3, song2026theimpactof pages 4-7) | More generated code does not necessarily lower total cost. Underwrite review, integration, security, and technical-debt capacity; effects vary by task, experience, and tool generation. |
| AI-crawler infrastructure load | Wikimedia reported that crawlers generated 65% of its most expensive traffic and that multimedia-download bandwidth grew 50% from January 2024—not that crawlers represented 65% of all requests. (noroozian2025generativeaiand pages 1-3) | Open access can create uncompensated compute and bandwidth liabilities. Budget for rate limits, bulk-data channels, authentication, caching, observability, and commercial access tiers. |
| Slop, triage burden, and cheaper replication | Across 294 popular repositories, 2025 PR volume was 6.8% above a modeled counterfactual and the one-time-contributor merge ratio was 18.18% lower; AI use was not directly observed. Only 11 of 1,786 maintainer-flagged slop PRs merged. Another study screened 575 possible open alternatives, but did not validate all matches or prove subscription churn. (raskin2026anempiricalstudy pages 5-6, afroz2026"aislopis pages 5-6, malo2026thecustomeris pages 15-16, raskin2026anempiricalstudy pages 9-11, raskin2026anempiricalstudy pages 3-4, afroz2026"aislopis pages 8-9, afroz2026"aislopis media 37156ac1) | AI lowers submission and prototyping costs, and plausibly imitation costs, but not necessarily validation, maintenance, or adoption costs. Do not generalize flagged slop to all AI-assisted PRs or treat repositories as proven substitutes. |


*Table: Measured evidence shows how generative AI can expand reuse and output while shifting traffic, infrastructure expense, and review work onto commons producers. The qualifications distinguish causal estimates from observational trends and prototypes from validated substitutes.*

## Where the value goes

**Open code becomes a model input.** BigCode assembled *The Stack* from approximately 3.1 TB of permissively licensed source code and used it to train the publicly released StarCoder family; StarCoderBase was trained on one trillion tokens from GitHub repositories. The project provided inspection, opt-out and attribution tools, illustrating a reciprocal model. Commercial coding assistants also draw on public-code ecosystems, but these studies do **not** establish how much of any assistant’s revenue is attributable to particular repositories or how much reaches their maintainers. A platform controlling the assistant, customer relationship and distribution can monetize capabilities derived partly from code maintained elsewhere. Public availability of code is not, by itself, evidence that every training or output use complies with its license. (kocetkov2022thestack3 pages 1-3, li2023starcodermaythe pages 1-2)

**Open science supplies inputs—and can receive valuable outputs.** Decades of publicly deposited protein structures and sequence research underpinned DeepMind’s AlphaFold. Google DeepMind and EMBL–EBI subsequently made more than 214 million predicted structures accessible through the AlphaFold database, which DeepMind funds: this is a substantial return to the research commons, not an example of a demonstrated AlphaFold subscription business. In biomedicine, the BIOMEDICA researchers converted over six million articles in PubMed Central’s open-access subset into more than 24 million image–caption pairs, then released a dataset, code and trained models. These examples show that the organization building an AI layer may gain model expertise, distribution or downstream application opportunities, while scientists and the public can also gain genuinely open assets; neither example quantifies a transfer of profit away from the original data stewards. (varadi2024alphafoldproteinstructure pages 1-2, varadi2024alphafoldproteinstructure pages 6-7, lozano2025biomedicaanopen pages 1-2)

That distinction matters economically: the costs of producing, validating, updating and serving source data remain with laboratories, repositories, publishers and contributors even when a downstream model makes the information easier to consume elsewhere. An analysis of reported AI training-data transactions found several pricing arrangements but that most documented deals excluded original creators from compensation; its deal sample should not be interpreted as a measured revenue share for *all* open-science or open-source producers. (oderinwale2510theeconomicsof pages 1-4)

## Demand, participation and operating costs

**AI answers can displace the visit and the public question.** A difference-in-differences study estimated that Stack Overflow’s weekly questions-and-answers fell about **16%** relative to comparison forums after ChatGPT launched, reaching roughly **25% within six months**. Votes on remaining posts did not materially improve, so the evidence does not support assuming that only trivial or low-quality contributions disappeared. A separate study found declines in Stack Overflow visits and questions but no comparable participation decline in the Reddit developer communities examined; it also found greater exit among newer Stack Overflow users. The loss at issue is not just a page view: a privately resolved question no longer automatically becomes a searchable answer, contributor interaction or fresh training example for the public commons. These are comparative observational studies, not proof that ChatGPT explains every subsequent decline. (riochanona2024largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, burtch2024theconsequencesof pages 5-7, burtch2024theconsequencesof pages 1-2)

Evidence for **documentation traffic specifically is narrower**. In a single-institution study of University of Ottawa library research guides—a form of open research documentation—**175 of 210** guides had fewer views across matched pre- and post-ChatGPT periods, with a **median change of −38.35%**. This is a before/after association, not a causal estimate for ChatGPT or a measured decline for software documentation generally. A separate study of requests to a developer-documentation endpoint shows why visits may also become a worse measure of consumption: AI agents can retrieve material in one or two requests instead of a human’s multi-page session. Thus an investor should examine human visits, machine retrieval and resulting product use separately rather than infer them from a single traffic chart. (lee2026changingpatternsof pages 1-3, lee2026changingpatternsof pages 3-5, borysenko2604developerexperiencewith pages 1-2)

**“Free to read” is not free to serve.** Citing its April 2025 operating report, researchers record Wikimedia’s finding that crawlers generated **65% of its most expensive traffic**, while bandwidth for multimedia downloads had grown **50% since January 2024**. The 65% figure refers to the costly traffic category—not 65% of all Wikimedia requests. In a separate, self-selected survey of 43 cultural-heritage institutions, 39 reported increased traffic and 27 of those attributed some or all of it to bots. Some operators reported disruptive bursts, but bot identity and purpose can be difficult to verify, and institutions experiencing trouble were more likely to respond. The investor-relevant exposure is variable bandwidth, capacity, bot mitigation and degraded service for human users, even where content remains openly licensed. (noroozian2025generativeaiand pages 1-3, weinberg2025areaibots pages 1-6, weinberg2025areaibots pages 14-18)

## Code production is cheaper; trusted integration is not automatically cheaper

Studies of Copilot find real contribution gains alongside extra coordination. One project-level analysis using GitHub usage data estimated **5.9% more OSS code contributions**, **3.4% more participating developers** and **8% more coordination time**; timely merges still increased overall. A Python-versus-R comparison found more package updates and disproportionately more maintenance-oriented than new-code contributions. In another study of Microsoft-owned open-source projects, peripheral contributors submitted more commits and pull requests while core contributors did more reviewing and fewer of their own commits. Designs, projects and outcome definitions differ, so these estimates should not be combined into a universal productivity rate. (song2026theimpactof pages 1-4, song2026theimpactof pages 4-7, yeverechyahu2024theimpactof pages 4-7, xu2025aiassistedprogrammingdecreases pages 3-5)

A randomized test provides an important counterweight: **16 experienced open-source developers**, assigned **246 tasks** in projects they knew well, took **19% longer** when permitted early-2025 AI tools. This does not negate the contribution gains above: task-completion time, code volume and the amount successfully integrated are different outcomes, and tools and users vary. Nor is *all* agent-generated work slop: a study of **567 Claude Code-assisted pull requests** across **157 projects** found **83.8%** were merged, although **45.1% of merged PRs** required further changes. That sample concerns identifiable agent-assisted PRs, not unsolicited submissions across the entire ecosystem. (becker2507measuringtheimpact pages 1-3, watanabe2026ontheuse pages 1-3)

**The risk is an asymmetry between cheap submission and scarce human judgment.** In an analysis of **294 active, popular repositories**, 2025 PR volume was **6.8% above** its modeled counterfactual and the one-time-contributor merge ratio was **18.18% below** it. The researchers did not observe AI use for each PR: concurrent ecosystem changes could contribute to either trend, and their issue-related results had weaker placebo-test support. A more targeted study identified **1,786 PRs explicitly flagged as AI slop by maintainers** across **76 affected repositories**; **11** were merged. That is evidence of a costly rejection queue, *not* evidence that only 11 of every 1,786 AI-assisted PRs are useful. Labels and maintainer judgments determine entry into this selected sample, and two repositories accounted for a large share. (afroz2026"aislopis pages 5-6, afroz2026"aislopis pages 8-9, afroz2026"aislopis media 37156ac1, raskin2026anempiricalstudy pages 3-4, raskin2026anempiricalstudy pages 5-6)

Bug reports show why blanket rejection has costs too. After low-quality vulnerability submissions drove curl’s confirmed rate below **5%**, it ended its bug-bounty program; later reporting put its confirmation rate near **16%** by April 2026. Across **120,918 reports** in **101 projects**, a 2026 study found AI-assisted reproduction and diagnosis associated with higher validity, but AI-generated reproducers were rejected more often than other reproducers (**23.53% versus 5.14%**). Maintainers therefore need reproducible evidence and triage capacity for both false alarms *and* genuine additional findings. (afroz2026"aislopis pages 1-2, liu2026copilotorculprit? pages 1-2, liu2026copilotorculprit? pages 2-3)

## Does AI make an open product easier to copy?

**Plausibly yes for implementation; not necessarily for a dependable replacement.** Agents can accelerate writing an alternative interface or reproducing observed functionality, while existing open components lower the initial build cost. A 2026 analysis found **575 screened candidate** open-source alternatives to twelve commercial products and rising rates of repositories describing themselves as alternatives. It explicitly cautions that some functional matches were unverified, that a rapidly built suite of applications had unverified completeness and reliability, and that repositories do **not** establish customer switching or lost subscription revenue. A reported organizational survey found that **32%** of respondents said their organization had forgone at least one software purchase or feature because it could build with agents; spending displaced and the quality of those builds were not measured. Verification, integrations, security, service and continued maintenance remain part of the make-or-buy calculation. Legal analysis likewise argues that AI is reducing the effort of reverse engineering, but that is not a measured rate of successful commercial cloning. (malo2026thecustomeris pages 1-3, malo2026thecustomeris pages 15-16, malo2026thecustomeris pages 18-21, mandel2026cheapaiassistedreverse pages 1-3)

## Implications for investors

1. **Underwrite the whole value chain, not repository popularity.** Identify who pays for curation and maintenance; who controls AI-facing discovery, customer distribution and usage data; and whether the producer receives fees, reciprocal contributions or other demonstrable returns. Open assets can create enormous public benefit without creating exclusive pricing power for their host. (li2023starcodermaythe pages 1-2, lozano2025biomedicaanopen pages 1-2, riochanona2024largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, oderinwale2510theeconomicsof pages 1-4)
2. **Stress-test demand and cost simultaneously.** Track human documentation and community participation separately from crawler/API requests; budget for bandwidth, caching, bulk access, rate limits, triage and maintainer retention. A growing number of AI fetches should not be booked as growing human adoption, and falling web visits need not mean the underlying data has become less useful. (lee2026changingpatternsof pages 1-3, borysenko2604developerexperiencewith pages 1-2, noroozian2025generativeaiand pages 1-3, weinberg2025areaibots pages 14-18)
3. **Test the defensibility of the *service*, not the difficulty of writing its code.** Vulnerability is greater where customers can substitute a narrow, easy-to-test feature. The investment case is stronger where value depends on continually refreshed, quality-controlled data, expert validation, integration into workflows, reliability, compliance, support or an enduring contributor network. This is an investment inference from the observed build-versus-buy limits, not a demonstrated ranking of companies. (malo2026thecustomeris pages 15-16, malo2026thecustomeris pages 18-21, becker2507measuringtheimpact pages 1-3, liu2026copilotorculprit? pages 2-3)
4. **Measure net, quality-adjusted output.** Require evidence on accepted contributions, time to review and deploy, defects, customer retention and maintenance cost—not generated lines of code or proposed PRs alone. Fund contribution gates and stewardship without indiscriminately closing newcomer pathways; both the productive agent-PR sample and the slop sample show why selection matters. (song2026theimpactof pages 1-4, becker2507measuringtheimpact pages 1-3, watanabe2026ontheuse pages 1-3, raskin2026anempiricalstudy pages 5-6, afroz2026"aislopis pages 8-9)

The resulting investment thesis is conditional: AI can expand the reach of open knowledge and reduce some production costs, while weakening traffic-based monetization and making unfunded hosting and verification less sustainable. The durable advantage is likely to lie in **trusted, continuously operated complements to openness**, rather than assuming that open code or open data alone guarantees either revenue capture or protection from imitation. (lozano2025biomedicaanopen pages 1-2, song2026theimpactof pages 1-4, noroozian2025generativeaiand pages 1-3, malo2026thecustomeris pages 15-16)

artifacts.artifact-00:
| Mechanism | Key measured observation | Investor interpretation and qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Open-code training and value capture | StarCoderBase was trained on 1 trillion tokens from permissively licensed GitHub repositories; its model and attribution tools were released publicly. The same open-code ecosystem supports commercial tools such as Copilot, but the evidence does not quantify how value is divided between vendors and contributors. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024) | Openness enables public innovation and private capture. Favor businesses with defensible workflow, distribution, support, or proprietary context—not merely access to open code. |
| Open-science data and reciprocal value | PDB’s open structures were indispensable to structure-prediction tools; Google DeepMind funds the open AlphaFold database, which contains over 214 million predictions. BIOMEDICA converted more than 6 million PMC articles into 24 million image-text pairs and released data, code, and models. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059) | Value is not solely captured privately: AI projects can return major research assets to the commons. Assess whether commercial beneficiaries fund stewardship and produce useful open outputs. |
| Lost Q&A and documentation traffic | Stack Overflow posts fell an estimated 16% relative to controls after ChatGPT, reaching about 25% within six months. In an observational Ottawa study, 175 of 210 research guides lost traffic; the median change was −38.35% across matched pre/post periods. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055) | AI can disintermediate audience, attribution, feedback, and contributor recruitment. The Stack Overflow result is quasi-experimental; the guide study does not prove that AI caused the decline. |
| Coding-assistant productivity and maintenance | Copilot use was associated with 5.9% more project-level OSS contributions but 8% more coordination time. In a separate randomized trial, 16 experienced developers completing 246 tasks in familiar projects were 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000030) | More generated code does not necessarily lower total cost. Underwrite review, integration, security, and technical-debt capacity; effects vary by task, experience, and tool generation. |
| AI-crawler infrastructure load | Wikimedia reported that crawlers generated 65% of its most expensive traffic and that multimedia-download bandwidth grew 50% from January 2024—not that crawlers represented 65% of all requests. (pqac-00000023) | Open access can create uncompensated compute and bandwidth liabilities. Budget for rate limits, bulk-data channels, authentication, caching, observability, and commercial access tiers. |
| Slop, triage burden, and cheaper replication | Across 294 popular repositories, 2025 PR volume was 6.8% above a modeled counterfactual and the one-time-contributor merge ratio was 18.18% lower; AI use was not directly observed. Only 11 of 1,786 maintainer-flagged slop PRs merged. Another study screened 575 possible open alternatives, but did not validate all matches or prove subscription churn. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000060) | AI lowers submission and prototyping costs, and plausibly imitation costs, but not necessarily validation, maintenance, or adoption costs. Do not generalize flagged slop to all AI-assisted PRs or treat repositories as proven substitutes. |


*Table: Measured evidence shows how generative AI can expand reuse and output while shifting traffic, infrastructure expense, and review work onto commons producers. The qualifications distinguish causal estimates from observational trends and prototypes from validated substitutes.*

info.query: How is generative AI changing the economics and risks of open-source software, open data and open science for the organizations that produce them? Include evidence on AI models trained on open code and open scientific data (who captures the value), declines in community Q&A and documentation traffic after ChatGPT (for example studies of Stack Overflow), effects of AI coding assistants on open-source contribution and maintenance, load from AI crawlers on open infrastructure, AI-generated low-quality contributions and bug reports burdening maintainers, and whether AI lowers the cost of copying or re-implementing open products. What do these imply for investors in open-source or open-science businesses?
